points: Protein contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, with small amounts of sulphur, phosphorus and iron in some proteins.
Protein is the only nutrient that contains nitrogen; carbohydrate and fat contain none.
Nitrogen is present in the amino group of every amino acid, so the nitrogen in a food comes from its protein.

notes.h: Basic structure of an amino acid
notes.b: Every amino acid has the same central carbon atom bonded to four groups. Only the side group differs between amino acids.
points: An amino group, -NH2, which carries the nitrogen.
A carboxyl group, -COOH, which gives the amino acid its acidic part.
A hydrogen atom.
A variable side group, labelled R, which gives each amino acid its identity.
The body builds its proteins from 20 different amino acids.
Diagram: a central carbon bonded to H, R, -COOH and -NH2, with R labelled as the side group that varies.
Essential amino acids cannot be made by the body in sufficient amounts, so they must be supplied by the diet.
Eight amino acids are essential for adults: lysine, leucine, isoleucine, valine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine and tryptophan.
Children also need histidine and arginine, which makes ten essential amino acids for children.
Non-essential amino acids can be made by the body from other amino acids and nitrogen-containing compounds, so food does not need to supply them.
Examples of non-essential amino acids: alanine, glycine, serine, aspartic acid, glutamic acid and proline.

notes.h: Peptides and the peptide bond (Higher Level only)
points: A peptide bond forms when the carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of another.
Water is released in this reaction, so peptide bond formation is a condensation reaction.
Two amino acids joined by one peptide bond form a dipeptide.
A peptide is a short chain of amino acids; a long chain is called a polypeptide, and a protein is made of one or more polypeptide chains.
Diagram: two amino acids joined by a peptide bond, with the -CO-NH- link and the water molecule released labelled.
Hydrolysis breaks a peptide bond by adding a molecule of water, which reverses the condensation reaction.
Repeated hydrolysis splits a polypeptide into smaller peptides and finally into free amino acids.
Enzymes such as pepsin and trypsin catalyse this hydrolysis in digestion, as covered in Digestion and Metabolism.

keyTerms.definition: A small organic molecule with an amino group and a carboxyl group, which are the building blocks of protein.
The -NH2 group of an amino acid, which carries the nitrogen in protein.
The -COOH group of an amino acid, which gives it its acidic part.
The variable part of an amino acid that distinguishes one amino acid from another.
An amino acid the body cannot make in sufficient amounts, so it must be supplied by the diet.
An amino acid the body can make from other amino acids and nitrogen-containing compounds.
The -CO-NH- link formed between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another, with water released.
The breaking of a chemical bond by adding water, as when peptide bonds are split during digestion.
A long chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.

questions.prompt: Name the elements found in protein and identify the four parts of the basic structure of an amino acid.
questions.model: Elements: carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, with small amounts of sulphur, phosphorus and iron in some proteins. Protein is the only nutrient containing nitrogen. Amino acid parts: an amino group (-NH2), a carboxyl group (-COOH), a hydrogen atom and a variable side group (R).

questions.prompt: Describe how two amino acids join to form a peptide bond, and explain how hydrolysis reverses this. Distinguish between essential and non-essential amino acids, giving one example of each.
questions.model: Peptide bond: the carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of another, releasing water (condensation); the bond is the -CO-NH- link; two amino acids joined form a dipeptide. Hydrolysis: a molecule of water is added to break the peptide bond, releasing the amino acids; enzymes such as pepsin and trypsin catalyse this in digestion. Essential amino acids cannot be made by the body in sufficient amounts and must be supplied by food; example lysine (eight essential for adults, ten for children). Non-essential amino acids can be made by the body from other amino acids and nitrogen-containing compounds; example alanine. Non-essential does not mean unimportant.
